references.text: The preceding verse provides the context: the disciples are to say, 'Peace be upon this house!' – verse 6 explains what happens with this greeting of peace depending on whether a 'child of peace' is there.

Jesus gives similar instructions in Matthew's mission discourse: if the house is worthy, peace will come upon it; if not, the peace will return to the disciples. The same principle regarding the return of peace applies.
The context for the greeting of peace upon entering a house in Matthew's version of the mission discourse.
Elisha sends Gehazi with the greeting, 'Peace be with you!' – an example of a greeting of peace sent to a household, with the idea that the peace is either received or not.
God's word shall not return empty but will accomplish what He sends it for. This parallels the thought that peace either rests upon the recipient or returns to the sender.
The psalmist prays for others, and if the prayer is not received, it returns to his own bosom – a parallel to the idea that peace returns to the disciples if it is not received.
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and says that what brings peace is now hidden from their eyes – an example of an offer of peace that is not accepted.

Paul and Barnabas state that God's word must first be proclaimed to the Jews, but since they reject it, the apostles turn to the Gentiles. A parallel thought: the message is offered, and rejection leads to its being taken further.
Paul shakes the dust from his clothes and says that the responsibility rests on the hearers' own heads – a similar principle that the preacher's responsibility ends upon rejection.
